dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?
Hi, yeah, good morning. Um, I'm calling about a fence. For my mother's house, I'm, I'm her daughter. Deirdre.
Okay, Deirdre. Tell me what you're thinking about for the fence and where the house is.

So it's twenty-six Ocean Avenue, out on the Ocean Drive side. And the road there is wicked busy, like, cars flying by all day, so she wants a stockade fence. You know, the solid kind, so she doesn't have to look at it all. Or hear it, I guess.
Sure. Stockade, so a solid privacy style. Is that going along the front of the property, facing the road?
Yeah, along the front. Well, wait, is stockade the one with the pointy tops? Or is that picket? I always mix those up.
Picket is the one with the spaced boards, usually lower. Stockade is the tall, tight, solid one. Sometimes the tops are pointed, sometimes flat.

Okay, so stockade. Got it. Although, um, the guy gave us a quote for black aluminum. Which I thought was not stockade, but he called it that? So I don't know. Anyway, black aluminum, and whatever is allowed tall. Like the tallest they let you.

Okay. So a solid-look panel in black aluminum, as tall as the city allows along the road. Height limits can be different for front yards versus side and back, so I'll want to check that against your zoning district.

Oh, it's different for the front? Huh. I didn't know that. Sorry, one sec. [pause] Sorry, I'm at work, I'm in the custodian closet at the school, there's a mop bucket right next to me, so if it echoes, that's why. I'm on speaker.
No problem at all, I can hear you fine. Go ahead.
Okay. So the main thing. Do I need to pull a permit before the guy starts? He says he just puts it up and it's no big deal, but that sounds, I don't know, sketchy?

In general, yes, a fence usually does need a permit here, so I'd hold off on having him start until that's sorted. The contractor may say it's no big deal, but the permit is typically the homeowner's responsibility too. Is your mother the owner on record?
Yeah, it's her name on the house. So she'd have to apply? Or can I do it? Because she's not great with the, like, online stuff.

Often a family member or the contractor can help with the paperwork, but she'd need to sign as the owner. I can have someone walk you through exactly what's needed. Did you have a question on the property line as well?
Yes! How close to the property line is allowed? Like can he put it right on the line? Because he said, quote, we'll just run it along the edge.

There's usually a required setback or a rule about being inside your own line, and the road side can have extra rules because of visibility for cars pulling out. I don't want to give you a number off the top of my head. Do you have a survey or a plot plan for the lot?
A survey? Um, maybe? Mom has a folder of stuff from when they bought it. Is that, like, a map with the little measurements?

Exactly, a drawing of the lot with measurements and the corners marked. If you can find that, it helps a lot. Also, is Ocean Avenue a city road in front of her house, do you know, or is there a sidewalk or a strip between the fence spot and the pavement?
There's a, like a grass strip, then the road. I don't know whose that is. Is that hers?

That's part of what we'd look at. Sometimes the strip is city right-of-way, so the line isn't where people assume. Let me take your number and have an inspector call you back with the height and setback for that spot.
Okay, it's four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-eight-four.
Four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-eight-four. And that's twenty-six Ocean Avenue, for a fence, under Deirdre Cullen.
Yep, that's it. So, wait, I tell the fence guy to wait, right? Not to start?
Sorry, I just want to be sure I'm getting it right.
Yes, tell him to wait until you've heard back and the permit question is settled. And look for that survey in the meantime.
Okay, thanks so much. I'll go dig through Mom's folder. Bye.
You're welcome, Deirdre. Take care.
